video.title: The Biggest NBA Surprise Shooting Risers & Fallers | Potential Busts Revealed

summary: Josh Lloyd covers year-to-year changes in shooting (3P%, rim finishing, 2P%, FG% and FT%) among top-200 fantasy players, using Dunks and Threes data that includes playoffs. His main point is that shooting categories are the most volatile in fantasy. They are rate stats with no floor, and 3P% quietly affects three categories. So a player's shooting should be described as what he did last season, not as a fixed trait. Players whose value was propped up by outlier shooting (Ayo Dosunmu, Jaylen Tyson, Bobby Portis, Christian Braun, Jarrett Allen at 70%) are flagged as regression risks. Players who fell (Aaron Nesmith, Paul George, Dyson Daniels, Domantas Sabonis) could bounce back. He is very confident Nesmith improves with Tyrese Haliburton back. He has worries about Onyeka Okongwu without Trae Young, and thinks Trae Young could surprise if his new efficiency holds.

rules.text: Free throw percentage, along with steals, is the most variable category from one year to the next. FG% and 3-point shooting also vary a lot.
rules.quote: the biggest variance category year-on-year is free throw percentage. And field goal percentage and three-point shooting is up there

rules.text: Shooting categories are rate stats with no floor. A bad shooter can keep dragging your team down, and you can lose a lead in the category on the last day of a matchup.
rules.quote: there's actually no floor to how bad you can be in shooting, which has a really negative impact on your team

rules.text: Don't label a player a bad shooter as a fixed fact. Frame it as how he shot last season. Only extreme cases like Giannis at the free throw line are near certain.
rules.quote: the way we always should be framing that stuff was or is he was a bad shooter last season

rules.text: 3-point percentage is a hidden category. It affects 3-pointers made, points and FG%. FG% and FT% each affect two categories.
rules.quote: three-point percentage is the biggest hidden category in in fantasy leagues, whether it's points leagues or category leagues

rules.text: Check whether a player's value is propped up by very high shooting numbers that may not hold, or whether he has room to improve.
rules.quote: would a player have scope to improve a lot, or has their value been, and I'll say this in American for you guys, buoyed

rules.text: Players whose fantasy relevance depends on elite shooting are risky because of how much shooting can vary.
rules.quote: when your game is relevant based on how well you shoot, and there's this much variance potential, well, it's a bit ugly

rules.text: Mid-range shooting is low volume, so it swings a lot. Rim finishing is higher volume and somewhat more predictable, but swings there matter more.
rules.quote: Mid-range shooting volume is low, so there tends to be more variance in the mid-range shooting.

rules.text: Rim finishing is only one part of FG%. An 11-point drop at the rim might cost about 3 points of overall FG%.
rules.quote: You might be losing three percentage points if you drop 11%, and 60 is still a okay number

rules.text: Players coming back from major injuries like ACL or Achilles tears almost always lose efficiency in their first season back.
rules.quote: that recovery from big injuries, ACLs and Achilles, it hurts players' efficiencies almost every time in their first run back

rules.text: If a 2-point percentage starts with a 7, expect it to come back down. Be skeptical of 70% field goal shooters in general.
rules.quote: If you see a number from two-point land that begins with a seven just expect it to come back.

rules.text: Teammates who create shots, like elite passers, can strongly affect a player's finishing and FG%.
rules.quote: Trae Young, one of the top five passers in the league, down to CJ McCollum and Nickeil Alexander-Walker. It's an impact.

rules.text: Overall 9-cat rankings can mislead. If you punt FT, a player's FT% getting worse barely matters to you, even if his rank falls a lot.
rules.quote: that's why I think your nine-cat rankings and total rankings and the way Yahoo displays it is misleading

rules.text: Unexpected free throw swings in either direction usually don't last and drift back toward the player's norm. You cannot predict them.
rules.quote: if someone kills your free throws or saves your free throws, especially if it's unexpectedly, probably not going to be a real thing
